opus-5.5.text:
I usually frame it in two layers. The first is what I'd call the "body" layer: perception, manipulation, locomotion, the basic ability to act reliably in the physical world. The second is the "brain" layer, meaning understanding, reasoning, planning, and especially generalization to situations the robot has never seen.

For a long time the field focused mostly on the first layer. People engineered a specific skill, like grasping a particular object or walking on a particular terrain, and got it to work very well in a narrow setting. That's valuable, but what I care about more is whether a robot can understand how the world works well enough to handle something new without being retrained from scratch.

That's why I come at robotics from the angle of world models. My background is in generative models and visual content generation, and I see a natural connection. If a model can generate the world, predicting what happens next when you push an object or open a door, then in some sense it understands the world's dynamics. That understanding is what a robot needs to plan and act. So the capability I care about most is less any single skill and more a general, predictive understanding of the physical world that many skills can be built on.

There's also a practical reason. Real-world robot data is very expensive and slow to collect. If we can build world models that let robots learn and rehearse in a simulated or generated environment, and then transfer that to reality, we change the economics of the whole field. So when I think about capabilities, I'm asking two things: can the robot generalize, and can we get there in a scalable way? Those two questions guide most of what I work on.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly frames capabilities in two layers—body and brain. Although it mentions perception, physical skills, and reasoning, it does not present them as a three-part decomposition.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually try not to start from the hardware. When people say "robot," they immediately picture arms and legs, and then the conversation becomes about degrees of freedom and gripper design. I come at it from the other direction, from vision and generative models, so for me the question is: what does an agent need to know about the world before its body even matters?

I usually break it into three layers.

The first is perception, and I mean it in a stronger sense than recognizing objects. It's building a representation of a scene that preserves geometry, physical properties, how things are arranged relative to each other. A cup on a table isn't a label, it's a thing with a position, a weight, a handle you can grasp from one side and not the other.

The second layer is what I'd call prediction, or really a world model. If I push this cup, what happens? If I let go of this door, does it swing back? Humans do this constantly and almost unconsciously. We've spent years on generative models of images and video, and the thing that excites me now is that a good video generation model is, in some sense, already a rough simulator of physics and causality. It has seen enough of the world to guess what comes next. That's exactly the capability a robot needs, because you can't afford to learn everything by trial and error on real hardware.

The third layer is action, closing the loop. Given what I perceive and what I predict, what do I do, and then how do I update when the world doesn't behave as expected. This is where the hard engineering lives, but I'd argue it's the layer that gets easier as the first two get stronger.

So when I frame the capabilities I care about, it's really this: can the system understand, imagine, and then act, in that order. Most of the robots we have today are strong on the third and weak on the second. My bet is that the breakthrough comes from the middle layer, from models that can dream about the consequences of their actions before they take them.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives a three-part breakdown: perception, prediction or a world model (the thinking component), and action that closes the loop, corresponding to physical execution.

astra-6.text: I’d frame them around three connected abilities: perceiving the world, acting in it, and learning from the results. A robot needs to understand what’s around it, translate a goal into physical actions, and recognize when those actions haven’t worked. The interesting part is how those abilities come together. If you ask a robot to pick up an object, it has to locate it, work out how to grasp it, and adjust if it slips. So I care about more than whether it can complete one demonstration. Can it handle a different object or an unfamiliar setting? Can it recover from a mistake? That adaptability is what makes a capability useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes perception, physical action, and learning from results. It does not clearly frame the capabilities as perception, thinking, and physical dexterity; learning is given as the third part instead.

sol-6.1.text: I think about three capabilities: perception, reasoning, and action. A robot needs to understand its surroundings, reason about what it should do, and then physically carry out that decision. And those capabilities need to work together. If you ask a robot to bring you a cup, recognizing the cup is only one part of the problem. It also has to figure out how to reach it, how to grasp it, and what to do if something changes along the way. What interests me is developing that complete loop, so robots can handle a range of tasks and adapt to situations they haven’t encountered before.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives a three-part decomposition—perception, reasoning, and action—and describes action as physically carrying out decisions, including reaching and grasping.
